title: Do vaccinated cases transmit measles? A systematic review and meta-analysis

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on whether vaccinated individuals can transmit measles virus and examines the characteristics of such transmission, including measles burden, number of doses, and time since vaccination. The central question is whether measles transmission occurs from vaccinated individuals and its implications for public health.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review conducted a systematic search of peer-reviewed and gray literature, identifying 11,911 records and including 33 articles. The meta-analysis calculated the median number of transmissions from vaccinated cases based on measles burden, number of doses, and time since vaccination.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Measles transmissions from vaccinated individuals, although relatively uncommon, can contribute to outbreaks. The meta-analysis found that vaccinated transmitters in eliminated areas were older than those in non-eliminated areas, and 91% of studies provided data on subsequent transmission generations, with a median of 4 cases per vaccinated transmitter.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that the evidence is limited in some areas, particularly regarding the age distribution of vaccinated transmitters and the mechanisms of transmission. There is also a need for more detailed studies on the role of vaccinated individuals in outbreaks.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Public health investigations should consider measles transmissions from vaccinated individuals, especially in areas where measles has been eliminated. Further research is needed to understand the dynamics of transmission from vaccinated cases and to improve outbreak response strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis investigate whether vaccinated individuals can transmit measles virus. The review included 33 articles from 11,911 peer-reviewed and 22 gray literature records. The meta-analysis found that vaccinated individuals can transmit measles, with a median of 4 secondary cases per vaccinated transmitter. Transmissions from vaccinated cases in eliminated areas were associated with older individuals compared to those in non-eliminated areas. The findings highlight the need to consider vaccinated transmitters in public health investigations and suggest areas for further research to better understand their role in outbreaks.

title: Operational drivers of measles outbreaks in Uganda: a multi-district outbreak causality analysis, July 2025– March 2026

analysis.scope_and_question: Measles outbreaks in Uganda persist despite the availability of an effective vaccine, suggesting persistent immunity gaps and health system weaknesses. The study focuses on identifying programmatic and health-system contributors to measles outbreaks and informing measles elimination programming.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A multi-district outbreak causality analysis (OCA) was conducted across 12 affected districts in Uganda (2025–2026), guided by the World Health Organization framework. The review involved deductive analysis of data to identify causal pathways and contributing factors.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Measles outbreaks were driven primarily by missed vaccination, especially incomplete delivery of the two-dose measles-rubella (MR) schedule, compounded by access barriers, delayed case detection, and limited outbreak preparedness. Findings were organized into four prespecified analytical themes: immunization service delivery, caregiver access and demand, surveillance and case detection, and outbreak preparedness and response.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study identified several limitations, including low clinical suspicion, limited engagement of Village Health Teams, laboratory and surveillance-information bottlenecks, absence of pre-positioned response plans, delayed response activation, and inadequate isolation capacity. These factors further limited early detection and control of outbreaks.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Strengthening routine MR1 and MR2 delivery, targeted catch-up vaccination, community-linked surveillance, and pre-positioned district response plans with clear activation triggers will be critical to closing immunity gaps and accelerating measles elimination in Uganda.

analysis.summary_en: This review article examines the operational drivers of measles outbreaks in Uganda through a multi-district outbreak causality analysis conducted between July 2025 and March 2026. The study highlights that measles outbreaks persist due to missed vaccinations, particularly incomplete delivery of the two-dose measles-rubella (MR) schedule, alongside access barriers, delayed case detection, and limited outbreak preparedness. The evidence base includes case investigation reports and qualitative interviews with district health teams, health workers, and community leaders. Key findings were organized into four themes: immunization service delivery, caregiver access and demand, surveillance and case detection, and outbreak preparedness and response. The study identifies several limitations, such as low clinical suspicion and inadequate isolation capacity, which hinder early detection and control. To address these issues, the authors recommend strengthening routine MR vaccination, implementing targeted catch-up campaigns, enhancing community-linked surveillance, and establishing pre-positioned response plans with clear activation triggers. These measures are critical for closing immunity gaps and advancing measles elimination efforts in Uganda.

title: Integrated Computational Design and Molecular Dynamics Evaluation of Novel siRNAs Targeting the Hemagglutinin Gene of Measles Virus

analysis.research_question_and_background: Despite the availability of an effective vaccine, measles virus (MV) remains a major global health concern because no approved antiviral therapeutics currently exist, and RNA interference (RNAi) studies targeting the conserved MV hemagglutinin (H) gene are limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used an integrated computational pipeline to identify and evaluate novel siRNA candidates targeting the MV H gene, starting with 96 MV strains for multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis.
analysis.methods: Eleven siRNA candidates were designed and screened for off-target effects, followed by thermodynamic analysis, secondary and tertiary structure prediction, hybridization energy evaluation, and molecular docking against human Argonaute-2 (hAgo2), with stability assessed via 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
analysis.main_results: The docking results showed that siRNA candidates S3, S4, and S7 displayed docking scores of -367.22, -349.03, and -383.07 kcal/mol, respectively, with favorable binding orientation within the catalytic PIWI domain of hAgo2, and maintained stable structural behavior throughout the simulations.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these findings as indicating that S3, S4, and S7 may serve as promising siRNA candidates against the MV H gene, representing a novel computational approach to antiviral development for measles.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings could inform the design of future antiviral strategies targeting measles, potentially addressing the unmet need for approved therapeutics and supporting the development of RNAi-based interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to computational predictions and simulations, with no in vitro or in vivo validation reported, indicating low strength and necessitating further experimental confirmation before clinical relevance can be assessed.

analysis.summary_en: This computational study aimed to address the lack of approved antiviral therapeutics for measles virus (MV) by designing and evaluating siRNA candidates targeting the conserved hemagglutinin (H) gene. Using 96 MV strains, the authors performed multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis to identify conserved regions, followed by the design of 11 siRNA candidates. These candidates underwent thermodynamic analysis, structural prediction, docking against human Argonaute-2, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations. The top three candidates (S3, S4, S7) demonstrated favorable docking scores and stable structural behavior, suggesting potential as antiviral agents. However, the study is limited to computational predictions without experimental validation, and the evidence strength is low, requiring in vitro and in vivo studies to confirm efficacy and safety.

title: Genetic characterization of production strains of measles, rubella, and mumps viruses by high-throughput sequencing

analysis.research_question_and_background: RNA viruses such as measles virus can accumulate spontaneous mutations that may compromise vaccine strain stability and efficacy, creating a need for genetic monitoring of production strains.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study characterized seed and production strains of measles (Leningrad-16), rubella (RA27/3), and mumps (Leningrad-3) viruses using high-throughput sequencing to assess genetic stability.
analysis.methods: Whole genome sequencing was performed on the MGI DNBSEQ G-400 and Illumina NextSeq2000 platforms, with data processed using FastQC, FastP, BWA-MEM2, and VizCoV tools to identify single nucleotide polymorphisms.
analysis.main_results: No SNPs were detected in the measles virus H protein, but a nonsynonymous polymorphism in the F protein was present in 30.0–40.9% of genomes; SNPs in rubella capsid C and E2 glycoprotein occurred up to 30%, and in mumps HN and F antigens occurred in less than 20%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret minor variant detection as evidence that high-throughput sequencing can monitor vaccine strain stability, highlighting its relevance for early detection of potential immunogenicity-altering mutations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support routine genomic surveillance of measles, rubella, and mumps vaccine production strains to ensure genetic stability and maintain vaccine immunogenicity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study did not evaluate functional effects of detected polymorphisms on vaccine immunogenicity, limiting causal inference; evidence strength is moderate given the absence of functional assays.

analysis.summary_en: This study used high-throughput sequencing to genetically characterize measles, rubella, and mumps vaccine production strains, comparing seed and production genomes to reference sequences. No mutations were found in the measles H protein, but a nonsynonymous F protein polymorphism occurred in 30–40% of genomes. Rubella and mumps strains showed minor variants in capsid and surface glycoproteins at frequencies up to 30% and less than 20%, respectively. The authors conclude that high-throughput sequencing enables monitoring of vaccine strain stability to detect early signs of potential immunogenicity changes. The work supports routine genomic surveillance of vaccine production strains to maintain product quality, though functional effects of detected variants were not assessed.

title: Association of Measles IgG Antibody Titers with Thoracic CT Severity in Hospitalized Patients with COVID-19

analysis.research_question_and_background: COVID-19 presents with a wide clinical spectrum, yet the influence of pre-existing anti-measles immunity on SARS-CoV-2 disease severity remains uncertain. The study sought to clarify whether anti-measles IgG titers are associated with clinical severity, mortality risk, ICU requirement, or thoracic CT involvement in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This cross-sectional study enrolled 153 hospitalized COVID-19 patients (86 males and 67 females) and classified disease severity according to NIH COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines.
analysis.methods: Anti-measles IgG levels were quantified using an indirect ELISA assay, and mortality risk was assessed with the COVID-19 Mortality Rate (CMR) score. Associations were evaluated after adjustment for clinical and laboratory parameters.
analysis.main_results: Higher anti-measles IgG titers were observed in patients with severe COVID-19 and severe thoracic CT involvement compared with milder cases. Anti-measles IgG titers remained independently associated with severe thoracic CT involvement after adjustment, but were not independently associated with mortality or ICU admission.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret anti-measles IgG titers as a potential immunological marker linked to pulmonary disease severity rather than mortality risk. This is the first report of an independent association between anti-measles IgG levels and severe thoracic CT involvement in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: If validated, anti-measles IgG titers could inform risk stratification for pulmonary complications in COVID-19, potentially guiding monitoring or therapeutic strategies in hospitalized patients.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and the single-center sample may reduce generalizability. The evidence is assessed as moderate due to these limitations and the absence of prospective validation.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study of 153 hospitalized COVID-19 patients found that higher anti-measles IgG titers were independently associated with severe thoracic CT involvement but not with mortality or ICU admission. Anti-measles IgG levels were measured by ELISA and severity was classified per NIH guidelines. The authors propose anti-measles IgG as a potential marker of pulmonary disease severity rather than mortality risk. The study is limited by its cross-sectional design and single-center setting, warranting prospective validation.

title: Clinical and epidemiological profile of suspected and laboratory-confirmed measles cases in South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, 2023

analysis.research_question_and_background: Measles continues to pose a public health burden in low-resource settings despite vaccination campaigns, creating uncertainty about post-campaign transmission dynamics and determinants of infection. The study addressed a knowledge gap on the clinical and epidemiological profile of suspected measles cases and factors associated with laboratory confirmation in South Kivu Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study was conducted in five health zones of South Kivu Province (Kalehe, Minova, Idjwi, Miti-Murhesa, and Kalonge) among children aged 6–59 months presenting with clinical signs of measles. Suspected cases were exhaustively enrolled from line lists provided by local health authorities.
analysis.methods: Blood samples were collected after obtaining parental consent and tested for measles and rubella IgM antibodies at the National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB). Data were analyzed using R version 4.3.3, and logistic regression was used to identify characteristics associated with measles IgM positivity among suspected cases.
analysis.main_results: Of the 82 children tested, 39 (48%) were positive for measles IgM. Among the 43 IgM-negative children, 8 (18%) were rubella IgM positive. In adjusted analyses, measles IgM positivity showed an association with male parental decision-making regarding child vaccination (aOR: 7.22; 95% CI: 1.64–43.2; p = 0.015) and other workers (aOR: 8.28; 95% CI: 1.19–48; p = 0.008).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating ongoing measles circulation despite high administrative vaccination coverage, highlighting the role of parental and community decision-making in vaccine acceptance. The novelty lies in identifying specific socio-behavioral factors associated with measles IgM positivity in a post-campaign setting.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that strengthening immunization service quality, improving outreach to unvaccinated children, and engaging male parents and other community workers may enhance vaccine acceptance and reduce measles transmission in the post-campaign period.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and the small sample size may reduce precision of effect estimates. The evidence is moderate due to potential selection bias from exhaustive line-list enrollment and unmeasured confounding in socio-behavioral factors.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study in South Kivu Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, examined 82 children aged 6–59 months with suspected measles to describe clinical and epidemiological characteristics and identify factors associated with measles IgM positivity. Blood samples were tested for measles and rubella IgM antibodies, with 48% testing positive for measles. Adjusted analyses revealed associations between measles IgM positivity and male parental decision-making regarding vaccination (aOR 7.22) and other workers (aOR 8.28). The authors conclude that despite high administrative vaccination coverage, measles continues to circulate, emphasizing the need to strengthen immunization services, improve outreach to unvaccinated children, and engage male parents and community workers to enhance vaccine acceptance and reduce transmission.

title: Universal screening for measles immunity during pregnancy: a cost-effectiveness analysis.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Measles is a highly contagious illness capable of causing significant morbidity and mortality, including adverse pregnancy outcomes. Routine screening for measles immunity is not currently recommended during pregnancy.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A decision-analytic model was constructed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of universal screening for measles immunity during pregnancy compared to usual care (ie, no screening for measles immunity). The model ran over two pregnancy cycles with a willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000 per QALY.
analysis.methods: Model inputs were derived from the literature.
analysis.main_results: Universal screening for measles immunity was the dominant strategy. Using a measles exposure rate of 0.1% to reflect the highest risk areas, the ICER of universal screening versus no screening was $166.46/QALY. When varying the measles exposure rate from 0.001-0.1%, screening remained the dominant strategy. During Monte Carlo simulation, measles screening for immunity during pregnancy was cost-saving and increased QALYs in 99.83% of simulations.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Universal screening for measles immunity during pregnancy is a cost-effective strategy. The findings demonstrate that the cost-effectiveness of the screening strategy is robust across a range of exposure rates.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Universal screening for measles immunity during pregnancy can inform public health policy by offering an opportunity for postpartum or preconception vaccination. It may also influence management of pregnant individuals who incur measles exposures.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on model inputs derived from the literature and does not include real-world data. The evidence strength is moderate due to reliance on assumptions and indirect data sources.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the cost-effectiveness of universal measles immunity screening during pregnancy in the United States. It highlights the potential benefits of identifying immunity status to guide postpartum or preconception vaccination, especially in areas with high measles exposure rates. The decision-analytic model shows that universal screening is a dominant strategy, with cost-saving and increased QALYs in most simulations. However, the study relies on literature-derived inputs and does not include real-world data, limiting its evidence strength to moderate. The findings suggest that universal screening could be a valuable tool in managing measles risks during pregnancy.

title: Characterizing Measles IgG-related Seroprevalence in the US Veteran Population during the 2025 West Texas outbreak.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Measles resurgence in the US raised concerns about population immunity gaps. The study addressed knowledge gaps on measles IgG seronegativity rates and testing patterns in the US veteran population during the 2025 outbreak.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A nationwide retrospective observational study was conducted using the US Veterans Health Administration (VHA) database. Veterans with measles IgG antibody testing performed from January through June in 2024 (pre-outbreak) and 2025 (outbreak) were included.
analysis.methods: Data were collected on measles IgG testing and serostatus during pre-outbreak and outbreak periods. Independent variables associated with seronegativity were determined using statistical models.
analysis.main_results: Measles IgG testing increased by 60.3% during the outbreak period (16,446 veterans tested). Seronegativity was 11.9% in the non-outbreak period and 9.18% in the outbreak period (p<0.0001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as identifying populations at higher risk of infection and transmission, particularly those with immune compromise. They highlighted the need for targeted interventions in these groups.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform vaccination strategies and targeted serologic screening in veterans, especially those with immunodeficiency or on Janus kinase inhibitors, to mitigate measles resurgence risks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's retrospective design and reliance on existing VHA data may limit generalizability and introduce selection bias. The evidence strength is assessed as moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This nationwide retrospective study assessed measles IgG seroprevalence in the US veteran population during the 2025 outbreak. Testing rates rose by 60.3% compared to the pre-outbreak period, with seronegativity decreasing from 11.9% to 9.18%. Independent risk factors for seronegativity included age ≤64 years, Janus kinase inhibitor use, and immunodeficient conditions. title: Barriers to disease notification among primary healthcare physicians in West Bank, Palestine: a cross-sectional survey

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines barriers to disease notification among primary healthcare physicians in the West Bank, Palestine, focusing on measles, mumps, and chickenpox as notifiable conditions. The central question addresses the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of primary healthcare physicians regarding notification of suspected measles cases, including factors associated with appropriate notification and barriers to timely reporting.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review reports a cross-sectional survey conducted among primary healthcare physicians in Palestinian Ministry of Health centers from August 2024 to May 2025. The study used a questionnaire to assess knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported notification practices, and applied multivariable logistic regression to identify factors associated with recent notification practices.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Among 223 respondents, 30.9% had good knowledge of the disease notification process, while 93.3% demonstrated a good attitude toward notification. Over 80% reported notifying their last-encountered measles, mumps, or chickenpox case, but timely notification was lower, with only 52.4% of measles cases reported immediately. Common misconceptions included the belief that laboratory confirmation is required for notification (61.0%) and that surveillance case definitions require laboratory criteria (65.5%).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Knowledge and attitude scores were not significantly associated with notification practices, potentially due to limited observations and composite scoring methods. The review highlights persistent underreporting despite positive attitudes, indicating unresolved barriers such as lack of time (60.5%), uncertainty about which diseases to notify (38.1%), and uncertainty about when to notify (32.3%).
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that strengthening training, clarifying guidance, improving feedback mechanisms, and addressing identified barriers may enhance disease notification performance by primary healthcare physicians in the West Bank. Specifically, physicians who received recent supervisory feedback had higher odds of notifying chickenpox cases (OR: 4.01, 95%CI: 1.40–11.43), and other medical specialties had lower odds of notifying mumps (OR: 0.21, 95%CI: 0.06–0.81) and chickenpox cases (OR: 0.23, 95%CI: 0.08–0.69).

analysis.summary_en: This review assesses barriers to disease notification among primary healthcare physicians in the West Bank, focusing on measles, mumps, and chickenpox. A cross-sectional survey of 223 physicians found that while 93.3% had positive attitudes toward notification, only 30.9% demonstrated good knowledge of the process. Over 80% reported notifying their last-encountered case, but timely notification was low, particularly for mumps (19.3%) and chickenpox (14.0%). Key barriers included lack of time (60.5%), uncertainty about which diseases to notify (38.1%), and misconceptions about laboratory requirements (61.0% and 65.5%). Supervisory feedback improved notification odds for chickenpox (OR: 4.01), while other medical specialties were less likely to notify mumps (OR: 0.21) and chickenpox (OR: 0.23). The review highlights the need for targeted training, clearer guidance, and improved feedback mechanisms to address underreporting.

title: ECHO: A lightweight tool for inferring missing case counts from pathogen phylogenies

analysis.research_question_and_background: Phylogenetic trees of pathogens provide evolutionary time scales but do not directly quantify unsequenced cases linked to an outbreak. analysis.study_design_and_population: The study introduces ECHO (Estimation of Cryptic Hosts from Outbreak trees), a tool comprising three lightweight estimators designed to infer missing case counts from timed phylogenetic trees. The authors demonstrate the tool’s performance through simulation and apply it to measles virus sequences collected during a 2021 outbreak in the USA.
analysis.methods: ECHO uses timed phylogenetic trees to relate total branch length to the total number of cases, thereby estimating cryptic cases. The tool is designed to be agnostic to sampling processes, ensuring robustness to heterogeneous sampling frameworks. Simulation studies and application to real-world measles virus data were used to evaluate accuracy.
analysis.main_results: ECHO recovered the number of cryptic cases with a reasonable degree of accuracy both in simulation and in practice when applied to measles virus sequences from the 2021 USA outbreak.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret ECHO’s estimates as providing actionable insights into the extent of cryptic transmission during outbreaks. The novelty lies in the development of a lightweight, sampling-agnostic tool specifically designed to infer missing case counts from phylogenetic data.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: ECHO can inform outbreak investigation and response by quantifying cryptic cases, thereby improving surveillance accuracy and guiding public health interventions for measles and potentially other pathogens with similar transmission dynamics.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report the specific sample sizes, statistical confidence intervals, or detailed limitations beyond the tool’s agnosticism to sampling heterogeneity. The evidence strength is moderate, as the findings are supported by simulation and a single real-world application.

analysis.summary_en: ECHO is a lightweight tool designed to estimate the number of cryptic cases linked to a pathogen outbreak using timed phylogenetic trees. The study addresses the gap in quantifying unsequenced cases by relating phylogenetic branch length to total case counts. ECHO comprises three estimators and is robust to heterogeneous sampling frameworks. The tool was validated through simulation and applied to measles virus sequences from a 2021 USA outbreak, demonstrating reasonable accuracy in recovering cryptic case counts. The authors interpret the estimates as providing actionable insights into cryptic transmission. ECHO has potential public health significance by improving surveillance accuracy and guiding interventions for measles and similar pathogens.

title: Routine early childhood vaccination uptake before and during the COVID-19 pandemic in Scotland: A population-based cohort study of administrative data.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed whether the COVID-19 pandemic altered routine early childhood vaccination uptake in Scotland, motivated by observed changes in family working patterns and increased vaccine focus during the pandemic.

analysis.methods: Timely uptake of six routine vaccinations was assessed using logistic regression to compare pandemic and pre-pandemic cohorts, with adjustment for sociodemographic variables and interaction analysis across area deprivation, parental socioeconomic class, urban-rural residence, and maternal ethnic group.
analysis.main_results: Vaccination uptake either remained stable or increased for five of the six vaccines during the pandemic, and most interaction terms were not statistically significant, indicating broadly similar effects across sociodemographic groups.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of resilience in Scotland’s childhood immunisation programme during the pandemic, while noting that large pre-existing inequalities persisted across socioeconomic and ethnic groups.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that routine early childhood vaccination programmes can maintain coverage during public health emergencies, but targeted strategies are needed to address structural barriers and reduce persistent inequalities.

analysis.summary_en: This population-based cohort study in Scotland evaluated whether the COVID-19 pandemic affected early childhood vaccination uptake by comparing pandemic and pre-pandemic cohorts using linked administrative health data for 199,574 children. title: Broad permissiveness of mammalian nectin-4 orthologs for morbilliviruses: a notable exception in dolphin nectin-4

analysis.research_question_and_background: Morbilliviruses utilize SLAM and nectin-4 as major receptors, yet host specificities remain poorly understood due to nectin-4's high conservation across mammals. This study aimed to investigate the role of nectin-4 in determining the host range of morbilliviruses, with a focus on measles virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study systematically compared the receptor activities of nectin-4 orthologs from human, dolphin, bat, dog, and seal for representative morbilliviruses, including measles virus, cetacean morbillivirus, canine distemper virus, phocine distemper virus, and Myotis bat morbillivirus.
analysis.methods: Cell–cell fusion, virus infection, and plaque assays were used to assess the receptor activities of nectin-4 orthologs. Mutational analyses identified specific amino acid residues that influenced receptor usage.
analysis.main_results: Most nectin-4 orthologs efficiently supported infection by all tested morbilliviruses, including measles virus. Dolphin nectin-4 showed markedly reduced receptor activity for measles virus, phocine distemper virus, and Myotis bat morbillivirus, but remained fully functional for cetacean morbillivirus and canine distemper virus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that nectin-4 is generally a broadly permissive receptor for morbilliviruses, but specific amino acid differences can significantly affect receptor usage, highlighting the importance of receptor compatibility in host range and cross-species transmission.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying measles virus host specificity and may inform strategies for understanding viral transmission and developing targeted interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only evidence, and while it identifies key amino acid differences, further experimental validation is needed to confirm the functional implications of these findings. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the limited scope of the analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of nectin-4 in determining the host range of morbilliviruses, with a focus on measles virus. It systematically compares receptor activities of nectin-4 orthologs from various mammals, revealing that most support infection by all tested viruses. However, dolphin nectin-4 shows reduced receptor activity for measles virus, phocine distemper virus, and Myotis bat morbillivirus, while remaining functional for cetacean morbillivirus and canine distemper virus. Mutational analyses identify amino acid residue 63 as a key determinant of receptor specificity. These findings highlight the importance of receptor compatibility in viral host range and cross-species transmission, offering potential insights for understanding measles virus behavior and informing future research. The study is based on abstract-only evidence, and while it provides valuable information, further experimental validation is needed to confirm its findings.

title: Prevalence and factors associated with immunization non-completion among children aged 12–23 months at Kisoro General Hospital, Uganda: a cross-sectional study

analysis.research_question_and_background: Immunization non-completion, defined here as a child missing at least one age-appropriate vaccine dose under Uganda’s national immunization schedule (UNEPI), remains a critical public health problem in sub-Saharan Africa, exposing children to preventable diseases.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study was conducted from October to December 2024 at Kisoro General Hospital among 275 caregivers of children aged 12–23 months attending the immunization clinic, selected by systematic random sampling.
analysis.methods: Data were collected via structured, pre-tested questionnaires and verified immunization card records. Descriptive statistics, bivariate chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression were performed using Stata version 15.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA).
analysis.main_results: The prevalence of immunization non-completion was 34.2% (94/275; 95% CI: 28.5–39.8%). In multivariable analysis, significant predictors included lack of formal caregiver education (aOR = 3.3, 95% CI: 0.93–11.49; p = 0.044), delayed initiation of immunization beyond three weeks of birth (aOR = 7.3, 95% CI: 3.66–14.72; p < 0.001), unfriendly health worker attitude (aOR = 5.8, 95% CI: 1.29–11.46; p = 0.022), and vaccine stock-outs (aOR = 6.1, 95% CI: 1.71–14.67; p = 0.005). Children of caregivers aged 25–34 years were less likely to have incomplete immunization than those of caregivers aged over 34 years (aOR = 0.3, 95% CI: 0.16–0.76; p = 0.008).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identified modifiable determinants at both caregiver and health system levels as significant factors associated with immunization non-completion.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Targeted interventions including caregiver education, timely postnatal vaccination, health worker training, and vaccine supply strengthening are urgently needed.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted at a single hospital in Uganda, which may limit generalizability. The evidence is moderate as it is based on a cross-sectional design and self-reported data.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted a cross-sectional analysis of immunization non-completion among children aged 12–23 months at Kisoro General Hospital in Uganda. It found that 34.2% of children had incomplete immunization, with significant predictors including lack of formal caregiver education, delayed initiation of immunization, unfriendly health worker attitudes, and vaccine stock-outs. The findings highlight the need for targeted interventions to improve immunization rates, such as caregiver education, timely postnatal vaccination, health worker training, and vaccine supply strengthening. However, the study's single-site design and reliance on self-reported data limit its generalizability, resulting in moderate confidence in the evidence.
